mainTopic: The rules of a valid fast: lasting until sunset, accepting it the day before, and eating the night before
overview: רב חסדא teaches that a תענית לשעות counts only if the person eats nothing until evening, even if he decided to fast only partway through the day. He adds a general rule: a fast that does not last until sunset is not a תענית at all. Three cases seem to prove otherwise: the אנשי משמר, the family of סנאה בן בנימין, and רבי יוחנן. Each is turned away as mere self-distress or a polite excuse. שמואל then rules that a fast must be accepted the day before, while it is still day. Someone who skips food without accepting the fast is 'like a bellows full of air.' רב and שמואל argue about whether the fast is accepted in the afternoon or during the מנחה prayer. A proof for שמואל from מגילת תענית is pushed off by reading 'ייסר' as 'יאסר', and that reading is explained as a rule about whether an earlier vow or an earlier decree wins. Finally, a ברייתא discusses how late one may eat the night before a daytime fast. אביי and רבא limit this, in two versions, by finishing the meal or by going to sleep. The definition of 'dozing' continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A partial-day fast counts only if one eats nothing until evening
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא limits the rule of מתענין לשעות. It only counts if the person tastes nothing until nightfall.
steps.simpleTranslation: That which you said, 'one may fast for hours,' applies only if he did not taste anything until the evening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a condition to the earlier rule that one may take on a fast 'for hours.' It counts only if the person eats nothing until evening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מתענין לשעות does NOT mean fasting for a few hours and then eating. It means that even if the fast was accepted only for the remaining hours of the day, those hours must run all the way to nightfall. This prepares the ground for רב חסדא's general rule in step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: fasting 'for hours': a fast accepted for only part of the day

steps.confusionAlert: A common mistake is to think תענית לשעות means fasting a few hours and then eating. Here it means the fast may start late in the day, but it must still last until evening.

phrases.english: That which you said, 'one may fast for hours'
phrases.notes: Refers back to the earlier statement (on the previous daf) that one may fast for part of a day.

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא שֶׁלֹּא טָעַם כְּלוּם עַד הָעֶרֶב.
phrases.english: is only when he did not taste anything until the evening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the earlier rule of מתענין לשעות from the preceding daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partial-day fast counts only if the person eats nothing until evening.

steps.title: אביי: that is just a regular full fast
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that if he ate nothing all day, this is obviously a full fast, so the rule teaches nothing new.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But this is a full-fledged fast!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רב חסדא's condition. If the person ate nothing until night, why call it a special 'fast for hours'? It is simply a complete fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is that the rule is obvious (פשיטא-style). If eating nothing until night is required, the case looks the same as an ordinary full-day fast, so מתענין לשעות seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: אביי, an אמורא who often challenges and clarifies

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
But this is a full-fledged fast!
phrases.notes: So what novelty is there in calling it 'fasting for hours'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: הָא תַּעֲנִית מְעַלַּיְיתָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the condition stated in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's condition that a תענית לשעות requires eating nothing until evening.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If nothing is eaten all day, it is simply a complete fast, so the category 'fasting for hours' seems pointless.

steps.title: The case is where he decided to fast only midway
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for someone who did not plan to fast in the morning, happened not to eat, and then decided midday to fast for the rest of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where he changed his mind (he decided to fast only in the middle of the day).
steps.whatsHappening: The answer explains the specific case. The person did not start the day intending to fast and only decided to fast later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is that a fast can count even if it was accepted partway through the day, as long as nothing was eaten before and nothing is eaten until night. That is what makes it different from an ordinary full fast, which is accepted from the start.

keyTerms.meaning: it is only needed for (a specific case)
he changed his mind / decided partway through

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where he changed his mind (decided midday to fast).
phrases.notes: He had not eaten yet, then accepted the fast for the remaining hours.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's objection by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation (אוקימתא): the rule applies to a fast accepted partway through the day.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think a fast only counts if it was accepted from the morning.
steps.terutzMaskana: A fast accepted midday, with no eating beforehand and none until night, is valid as a תענית לשעות.
steps.whatToRemember: תענית לשעות = a fast accepted partway through the day, but still kept until nightfall with nothing eaten all day.

steps.title: A fast that does not last until sunset is not a fast
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא's general rule: if one eats before sunset, it does not count as a תענית at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: Any fast upon which the sun did not set is not called a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא states a broad rule. A fast must last until sunset, or it is not a fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits step 1, where a partial fast had to last until evening. Now it is stated as a general definition: ending a fast early takes away the status of תענית completely, not just partly. The rest of this passage tests this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: רב חסדא, the אמורא making these rulings
the sun set upon it (it lasted until sunset)
it is not called a fast

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the halachic definition of a valid fast. The three challenges that follow all try to undermine it.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁלֹּא שָׁקְעָה עָלָיו חַמָּה —
phrases.english: Any fast upon which the sun did not set
is not called a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: כׇּל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁלֹּא שָׁקְעָה עָלָיו חַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, related statement of רב חסדא that generalizes the condition in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fast that is broken before sunset is not considered a fast.

steps.title: Challenge from the priestly watch who fast but do not finish
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the אנשי משמר fast but do not complete the fast, which suggests a partial fast is still called a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: The members of the priestly watch fast but do not complete the fast!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא with a source. The כהנים serving that week 'fast' even though they stop before evening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source uses the word 'fast' (מתענין) for something that ends early. That seems to contradict רב חסדא's claim that such a thing is not called a fast at all.

keyTerms.meaning: they raised an objection (from a תנאי source)
the כהנים of the rotation serving in the בית המקדש that week

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
The members of the priestly watch fast but do not complete it!
phrases.notes: They stop early so they have strength for the עבודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: אַנְשֵׁי מִשְׁמָר מִתְעַנִּין וְלֹא מַשְׁלִימִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב חסדא's rule from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's rule that a fast not lasting until sunset is not a fast.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls an incomplete fast 'fasting,' so a partial fast does seem to be a fast.

steps.title: They were only distressing themselves
steps.stepSummary: The אנשי משמר were not keeping a real fast. They held back from food only to share in the community's distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is merely to cause himself distress.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משמר's 'fast' was not a real fast. It was just a personal act of discomfort.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'fast' in the ברייתא is used loosely. It describes holding back from food in solidarity, not a halachic תענית. So רב חסדא's definition is untouched.

phrases.english: There, it is merely to cause himself distress.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the source's case: the act was distress, not a halachic fast.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's use of 'fast' shows a partial fast is a real fast.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משמר only held back from food as an act of distress, so רב חסדא's rule stands.

steps.title: Challenge from the family of סנאה on a postponed תשעה באב
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק reports that his family fasted on the postponed תשעה באב but did not finish, because that day was their family יום טוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק said: I am a descendant of סנאה בן בנימין. Once תשעה באב fell on שבת and we postponed it until after שבת. We fasted on it but did not complete it, because it is our יום טוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source against רב חסדא. A family 'fasted' on תשעה באב without completing the fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The family's private festival (they brought wood for the מזבח on the 10th of Av) stopped them from finishing, yet רבי אלעזר still calls it 'we fasted.' That again suggests a partial fast is a fast. This source is stronger than the last one, because it concerns the real public fast of תשעה באב.

keyTerms.meaning: come and hear (a source is being brought)
a family from שבט בנימין with a family festival

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק:
phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנִי מִבְּנֵי בָנָיו שֶׁל סְנָאָה בֶּן בִּנְיָמִין,
phrases.english: I am of the descendants of Senaah son of Benjamin,

phrases.aramaic: וּפַעַם אַחַת חָל תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב לִהְיוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת,
phrases.english: and once the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat,
and we postponed it until after Shabbat,
phrases.notes: So the fast fell on the 10th of Av, their family festival.

phrases.english: and we fasted on it but did not complete it
because it is our holiday.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רב חסדא's rule, after the first was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's rule that a fast not lasting until sunset is not a fast.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A תנא calls a partial תשעה באב fast 'we fasted,' implying partial fasts count.

steps.title: That too was merely self-distress
steps.stepSummary: The same answer applies: the family only held back from food as an act of distress, not as a real fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, it is merely to cause himself distress.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as in step 6. The family's partial fast was only an act of distress.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since they could not keep a real fast on their יום טוב, they held back for part of the day only to show mourning. Calling it 'fasting' does not make it a halachic תענית.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם נָמֵי, לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּעָלְמָא הוּא.
phrases.english: There too, it is merely to cause himself distress.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּעָלְמָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 with the same reasoning as step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Same redefinition: distress, not a real fast.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The family's partial fast was a real fast.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was only self-distress, so רב חסדא is not contradicted.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן's fast until reaching home
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן would say 'I will fast until I come home,' which suggests one can accept a fast for just a few hours.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יוחנן said: I shall be in a fast until I come to my house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third challenge. רבי יוחנן accepted a fast that would end when he got home, well before sunset.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here a great אמורא explicitly takes on a short fast with a set ending. That looks like clear proof that a fast ending before sunset is still a fast.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יוחנן, a leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל
I shall be in a fast

phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
I shall be in a fast until I come to my house.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֱהֵא בְּתַעֲנִית עַד שֶׁאָבוֹא לְבֵיתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge to רב חסדא's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's rule that a fast not lasting until sunset is not a fast.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן accepted a fast with an early endpoint, implying a short fast is valid.

steps.title: He was only excusing himself from the נשיא's meal
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's 'fast' was a polite way to turn down a meal at the נשיא's house, not a real fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he did it to excuse himself from the house of the נשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the third challenge. רבי יוחנן's words were a polite excuse to avoid dining with the נשיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I am fasting' let him decline without insulting the נשיא, and then he ate at home. It was never a halachic תענית, so רב חסדא's rule stands after all three challenges.
steps.whatToRemember: All three challenges are turned away. A fast that does not last until sunset is not a real תענית. Partial 'fasts' in the sources were only self-distress or a polite excuse.

phrases.english: There, to excuse himself
from the house of the Nasi is why he did it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, לְשַׁמּוֹטֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ מִבֵּי נְשִׂיאָה הוּא דַּעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: a polite excuse, not a fast.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן truly accepted a short fast.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was only a way to decline the נשיא's invitation, so there is no proof against רב חסדא.

steps.title: שמואל: A fast must be accepted while it is still day
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that a fast not accepted while it is still day, the day before, does not count as a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Any fast that a person did not take on himself while it was still day is not called a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל states the basic rule. To count as a real fast, a fast must be accepted ahead of time, on the day before, while it is still daytime.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new rule, separate from רב חסדא's. רב חסדא spoke about when a fast must END (it must last until sunset). שמואל speaks about when it must be ACCEPTED: the day before, in daylight. Without that acceptance, not eating is simply not a תענית.

keyTerms.meaning: took upon himself (formally accepted the fast)
while it is still day (on the previous day, before nightfall)
it is not called / it does not count as

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the well-known halacha that a personal fast must be accepted on the day before.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁלֹּא קִיבֵּל עָלָיו מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם —
phrases.english: Any fast that one did not take upon himself while it was still day —
is not called a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: כׇּל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁלֹּא קִיבֵּל עָלָיו מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new statement by שמואל about when a fast must be accepted. It is independent of רב חסדא's rule about the fast lasting until sunset.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fast counts only if it was accepted on the previous day while it was still daytime.

steps.title: What if he sat without eating anyway?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the status is of someone who did not accept the fast in advance but still went the whole day without eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he sat (fasting) anyway, what is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about שמואל's rule. It sets up the next line, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said such a day is 'not a fast.' The question is what it is, then. Does the person get anything at all for his effort of not eating?

keyTerms.meaning: and if he sat (went the day without eating)

phrases.english: And if he sat [in a fast], what is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up question about the practical result of שמואל's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the status is of someone who goes the day without eating but never accepted the fast in advance.

steps.title: Like a bellows full of air
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר שילא answers that such a person is like a bellows filled with air: he is empty of food, but he has not fasted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר שילא said: He is like a bellows that is full of air.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר שילא answers the question with a picture. Someone who does not eat without having accepted the fast is just 'empty,' like a bellows blown full of air.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bellows full of air has nothing real inside it. In the same way, this person's day without food has none of the substance of a real תענית. He was hungry, but he did not fast.

keyTerms.meaning: a bellows (the tool used to blow air into a fire)

phrases.english: Rabba bar Sheila said:
He is like a bellows that is full of air.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר שֵׁילָא: דָּמֵי לְמַפּוּחָא דְּמַלְיָא זִיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not eating without having accepted the fast has no value as a fast. It is just being empty, like a bellows full of air.

steps.title: When exactly is the fast accepted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks at what point on the previous day a person accepts the fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: When does one accept it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about timing. It sets up the argument between רב and שמואל in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know the fast must be accepted 'while it is still day.' But that could be any time during the day. The גמרא wants the exact time.

phrases.english: When does one accept it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows שמואל's 'while it is still day' to an exact time.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact time on the previous day when the fast must be accepted.

steps.title: רב: in the afternoon; שמואל: in the מנחה prayer
steps.stepSummary: רב says the fast is accepted during מנחה time (the afternoon). שמואל says it is accepted during the מנחה prayer itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: During the afternoon. And שמואל said: During the מנחה prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: Two answers are given to the question of when the fast is accepted. רב says any time in the afternoon. שמואל says it must be done inside the מנחה prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the time matters: once it is afternoon, he can accept the fast. For שמואל, the setting matters: the acceptance belongs inside the תפילה of מנחה.

keyTerms.meaning: in the afternoon (the time of מנחה)

steps.confusionAlert: Both answers use the word 'מנחה,' but they are different. רב means the TIME of the afternoon. שמואל means the actual PRAYER of מנחה.

phrases.english: Rav said: In the afternoon,
And Shmuel said: In the afternoon prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: בְּמִנְחָה, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בִּתְפִלַּת הַמִּנְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two competing answers to the timing question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: the afternoon (מנחה time). שמואל: during the מנחה prayer.

steps.title: רב יוסף supports שמואל from מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says שמואל's view makes sense, and brings a line from מגילת תענית that ends with the word 'ייסר'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: It makes sense like שמואל, as it is written in מגילת תענית: 'Therefore, any person who took upon himself beforehand — ייסר (he will be bound).'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a written source to back שמואל. He quotes the closing line of מגילת תענית about someone who took a fast on himself beforehand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מגילת תענית lists festive days on which fasting is not allowed. Its closing line speaks about a person who committed to a fast beforehand, ending with the word 'ייסר.' The next step shows how רב יוסף reads that word as a link to the מנחה prayer.

keyTerms.meaning: it stands to reason in accordance with (him)
an early scroll listing festive days on which fasting is forbidden
he will bind (himself) / he will be bound

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
It stands to reason like Shmuel,
as it is written in Megillat Taanit:
Therefore, any person who takes upon himself
beforehand — he will be bound.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: כְּווֹתֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דִּכְתִיב בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to decide the רב and שמואל argument in שמואל's favor.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's view that the fast is accepted during the מנחה prayer.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The closing line of מגילת תענית: 'כל אינש דייתי עלוהי מקדמת דנא ייסר.'

steps.title: Spelling out the proof: he binds himself in his prayer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the proof: 'ייסר' means he binds himself to the fast in his prayer (בצלו), which matches שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it not that 'ייסר' means he binds himself in his prayer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the word 'ייסר' is supposed to prove שמואל's view. It is read as 'he binds himself in his prayer.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depends on reading 'ייסר' as binding oneself to the fast, and doing it through תפילה. If that reading holds, acceptance happens during prayer, just as שמואל says.

keyTerms.meaning: is it not that…? (introduces a suggested reading used as a proof)

phrases.english: Is it not — he binds himself in his prayer?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out exactly how the quoted line supports שמואל.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל: acceptance happens during the מנחה prayer.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Reading 'ייסר' as 'he binds himself in his prayer.'

steps.title: No: read it as 'he is forbidden'
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The word should be read 'יאסר,' meaning 'he will be forbidden.' The line is about a prohibition (explained in step 21), so it says nothing about prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: No — 'יאסר' means he forbids himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by changing how the word is read. With a one-letter change, 'ייסר' becomes 'יאסר,' meaning 'he is forbidden.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the new reading, the line is about a prohibition that binds someone who took on a fast beforehand. Step 21 spells out exactly what that means. The line no longer speaks about how a fast is accepted, so it gives no support to שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: he will be forbidden (under a prohibition; step 21 explains what is forbidden)

steps.confusionAlert: 'ייסר' and 'יאסר' look and sound almost the same, but they mean different things. 'ייסר' = he binds himself (here, read as binding himself in prayer). 'יאסר' = he becomes forbidden, a prohibition that has nothing to do with prayer.

phrases.english: No — he renders himself forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 17 by rereading the key word.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from מגילת תענית is rejected. שמואל's view itself is not disproven.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof depends on reading 'ייסר.' It can be read 'יאסר,' a prohibition that has nothing to do with prayer.

steps.title: רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argue over the reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports that רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argue about this very reading. One says 'ייסר' and the other says 'יאסר.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argue about this. One said: ייסר. And one said: יאסר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the two readings from the last steps are not just guesses. They were a real argument between two early sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both readings now have an authority behind them. The text says 'one said… and one said' without telling us who held which view. This sets up the next step's question about what each reading means.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי שמעון, son of רבי (יהודה הנשיא)

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּרַבִּי.
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi disagree about it.
One said: 'He will be bound,'
and one said: 'He will be forbidden.'

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the two readings from steps 16 to 18 were an actual argument between early sages.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is an earlier dispute over whether מגילת תענית reads 'ייסר' or 'יאסר.'

steps.title: What does the 'יאסר' reading mean?
steps.stepSummary: The 'ייסר' reading is explained as already discussed. The גמרא asks what the 'יאסר' reading means.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who said 'ייסר,' it is as we said. According to the one who said 'יאסר,' what is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the 'ייסר' reading is already clear: binding oneself to the fast in prayer. It then asks for the meaning of the other reading. This sets up an explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'ייסר' reading was explained in step 17. The 'יאסר' reading needs a clear case: who exactly is forbidden, and in what situation? The next step answers this from מגילת תענית.

keyTerms.meaning: what is it? (what does it mean?)

phrases.english: The one who said 'he will be bound' — it is as we said.
According to the one who said 'he will be forbidden' — what is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר יֵיסַר — כִּדְאָמְרִינַן. לְמַאן דְּאָמַר יֵאָסֵר — מַאי הִיא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to explaining the second reading in the dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact case and meaning of the 'יאסר' reading in מגילת תענית.

steps.title: The 'יאסר' reading explained: whichever came first, the vow or the decree, wins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from step 20 by quoting the full line from מגילת תענית. The reading 'יאסר' means that someone whose vow to fast came first is bound by it. The ברייתא then explains with a case: a vow made before the decree overrides the decree, and a decree made before the vow overrides the vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in מגילת תענית: Any person who took upon himself (a fast) beforehand will be forbidden (to eat). How so? An individual accepted upon himself to fast every Monday, Thursday, and Monday all year long, and the festive days listed in מגילת תענית fell on those days. If his vow came before our decree, his vow cancels our decree. If our decree came before his vow, our decree cancels his vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the 'יאסר' reading by quoting the full source, which talks about timing (vow before decree) and has nothing to do with prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the 'יאסר' reading, 'מקדמת דנא' means 'before the decree,' not 'before the fast day in his prayer.' So the line teaches which rule wins, the earlier vow or the earlier decree. This is why the 'יאסר' reading cannot serve as a proof for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: An ancient list of happy days on which fasting is not allowed
He will be forbidden (here: forbidden to eat, so he must keep his fast)
Our decree (the rabbis' ruling that these days are festive)

steps.whatToRemember: In the 'יאסר' reading, 'beforehand' is about timing. An earlier vow beats the decree, and an earlier decree beats the vow.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'יאסר' means forbidden to EAT, so his vow stands and he fasts. It does not mean he is forbidden to fast. Only when the decree came first is he barred from fasting.

phrases.english: As it is taught in Megillat Taanit:
Any person who brings upon himself (a fast)
beforehand will be forbidden (to eat).
How so?
An individual who accepted upon himself
Monday, Thursday, and Monday
of the entire year,
and festive days fell on them
that are written in Megillat Taanit,
if his vow came before our decree,
his vow cancels our decree,
and if our decree came before his vow,
our decree cancels his vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20 about what the 'יאסר' reading means.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'יאסר' refers to a vow made before the decree. Such a vow overrides the decree, and a decree made first overrides a later vow.

steps.title: Until when may one eat on the night before a fast
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: for a fast that begins in the morning, one may eat during the night. רבי says until dawn. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says until the rooster crows.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Until when may one eat and drink? Until dawn rises. These are the words of רבי. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says: Until the rooster calls.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about the latest time one may eat before a daytime fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This applies to fasts that do not start the evening before. רבי allows eating all the way to dawn. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון sets an earlier cutoff, the rooster's call, which comes before dawn.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Until when may one eat and drink?
Until dawn rises,
the words of Rabbi.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says:
Until the rooster calls.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: עַד מָתַי אוֹכֵל וְשׁוֹתֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the מגילת תענית discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may eat before a daytime fast until dawn (רבי) or until the rooster's call (רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון).

steps.title: אביי: finishing the meal ends the right to eat
steps.stepSummary: אביי limits the ברייתא: one may eat all night only while still in the middle of the meal. Once he has finished his meal, he may not eat any more.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: They taught this only when he did not finish his meal. But if he finished his meal, he does not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds a condition to the ברייתא: eating all night is allowed only if the meal has not ended.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Finishing the meal is treated as a mental 'closing,' as if he has already accepted the fast. After that, starting to eat again is not allowed, even before dawn.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in a case where (a limiting phrase)

phrases.english: Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא גָּמַר סְעוּדָתוֹ,
phrases.english: They taught this only when he did not finish his meal,
but if he finished his meal, he does not eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ברייתא of step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating through the night is allowed only if the meal was not finished.

steps.title: רבא challenges: a ברייתא says one who finished may still eat
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes a ברייתא: if one finished and stood up, he may still eat. This seems to contradict אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenged him: 'If he finished and stood up, he may eat!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's condition with a ברייתא that allows eating even after finishing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said finishing the meal ends eating. The ברייתא says someone who 'finished and stood up' may still eat, which looks like the exact opposite.

phrases.english: Rava challenged him:
If he finished and stood up, he may eat!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's statement in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's rule that finishing the meal ends eating.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly allows eating after finishing and standing up.

steps.title: Answer: the table was not yet cleared
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about a case where the table was not yet cleared, so the meal is not truly over.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is when he did not clear away (the table).
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that the ברייתא is about someone whose table had not yet been cleared.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing up alone does not end a meal. As long as the food or table is still there, the meal counts as ongoing, so he may still eat. The meal truly ends only when the table is cleared.

phrases.english: There, it is when he did not clear away (the table).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Finished and stood up' means the meal was fully over.
steps.terutzMaskana: The table was not cleared, so the meal had not truly ended.

steps.title: Second version: רבא says sleeping ends the right to eat
steps.stepSummary: Some report the discussion differently: רבא says one may eat all night only if he did not go to sleep. Once he slept, he may not eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רבא said: They taught this only when he did not sleep. But if he slept, he does not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of the discussion, in which the limit is sleep rather than finishing the meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, going to sleep is the act that 'closes' the eating period. Finishing the meal is not mentioned, and here it is רבא who sets the condition.
steps.confusionAlert: In this version the roles are switched: רבא makes the statement and אביי asks the challenge.

phrases.english: Some say: Rava said:
They taught this only when he did not sleep,
but if he slept, he does not eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternate version of the limit on the ברייתא from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating through the night is allowed only if he did not go to sleep.

steps.title: אביי challenges: a ברייתא says one who slept may still eat
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא: if one slept and got up, he may eat. This seems to contradict רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי challenged him: 'If he slept and got up, he may eat!'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's condition with a ברייתא that allows eating after sleeping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said sleep ends the eating period. The ברייתא says someone who 'slept and got up' may still eat.

phrases.english: Abaye challenged him:
If he slept and got up, he may eat!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's statement in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that sleeping ends eating.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly allows eating after sleeping and getting up.

steps.title: Answer: he was only dozing
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about someone who was only dozing, not truly asleep.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is about one who was dozing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers that the ברייתא is about light dozing, not real sleep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real sleep ends the eating period. A light doze does not, so the ברייתא allows eating after it. The ברייתא's word 'slept' is read as 'dozed.'

phrases.english: There, it is about one who was dozing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the ברייתא
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only dozing, which does not end the eating period.

steps.title: What exactly counts as dozing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a definition of 'dozing' and begins רב אשי's answer, which continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case of dozing? רב אשי said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how to tell dozing apart from real sleep. This sets up רב אשי's answer, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the law now depends on the difference between sleep and dozing, a clear definition is needed. Only the attribution to רב אשי appears here, and his actual definition follows on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?

phrases.english: What is the case of dozing?
Rav Ashi said:
phrases.notes: Introduces the answer, which continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the term used in the answer of step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A definition of 'dozing' as opposed to real sleep.
